la:verb:colo.html:
cŏlo, colŭi, cultum, 3, v. a.
from the stem ΚΟΛ, whence βουκόλος, βουκολέω; cf.: colonus, in-cola, agri-cola
(orig. pertaining to agriculture),
to cultivate, till, tend, takecare of a field, garden, etc. (freq. in all per. and species of composition).
Prop.
With acc.: fundum,: agrum,; ; pr.: agri non omnes frugiferi sunt qui coluntur,; : arva et vineta et oleas et arbustum,: praedia,: rus,: rura,; ; : hortos,: jugera, pr.: patrios fines,: solum,: terram,: arbustum,: vitem,: arbores,: arva,; : fructus,: fruges,: poma,; cf. under P. a.—
Absol., ; ; .—
In gen., without reference to economics, to abide, dwell, stay in a place, to inhabit (syn.: incolo, habito; most freq. since the Aug. per.).
With acc.: hanc domum,: nemora atque cavos montes silvasque colebant,: regiones Acherunticas,: colitur ea pars (urbis) et habitatur frequentissime,: urbem, urbem, mi Rufe, cole,: has terras,; : loca Idae,: Idalium,; : urbem Trojanam,: Sicaniam,: Maeoniam Sipylumque,: Elin Messeniaque arva,: regnum nemorale Dianae,: hoc nemus,: Elysium,: loca magna,; : Britanniam,: Rheni ripam,: victam ripam,: terras,; cf. : insulam,; : regionem,.—Poet., of poets: me juvat in primā coluisse Helicona juventā,i. e. to have written poetry in early youth,—Also of animals: anguis stagna,; .—

Trop. (freq. and class.).
To bestow care upon a thing, to care for.

Of the body or its parts, to cultivate, attend to, dress, clothe, adorn, etc.: formamque augere colendo,by attire, dress,: corpora,: tu quoque dum coleris,.—With abl.: lacertos auro,: lacertum armillā aureā,: capillos,; .—
With abstr. objects, to cultivate, cherish, seek, practise, devote one's self to, etc.; of mental and moral cultivation: aequom et bonum,: amicitiam,: fidem rectumque,: fortitudinem,: jus et fas,: memoriam alicujus,: bonos mores,: suum quaestum colit,: pietatem,; : virtutem,; : amicitiam, justitiam, liberalitatem,: virginitatis amorem,: pacem,; cf. Martem, Sil.

Colere aliquem, to regard one with care, i. e. to honor, revere, reverence, worship, etc. (syn.: observo, veneror, diligo).

Of the honor bestowed upon men: ut Africanum ut deum coleret Laelius,: quia me colitis et magnificatis,; : a quibus diligenter observari videmur et coli,; cf. ; ; ; : poëtarum nomen,: civitatem,; cf.: in amicis et diligendis et colendis, and 82: semper ego plebem Romanam militiae domique... colo atque colui,: colere et ornare,: me diligentissime,init.: si te colo, Sexte, non amabo,: aliquem donis,: litteris,: nec illos arte colam, nec opulenter, Kritz.— Hence,
cŏlens, entis, P. a., honoring, treating respectfully; subst., a reverer, worshipper; with gen.: religionum,.—
cultus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to I.).
Cultivated, tilled: ager cultior,: ager cultissimus,: materia et culta et silvestris,: res pecuaria,: rus cultissimum,: terra,: fundus cultior,: cultiora loca,.—
Subst.: culta, ōrum, n., tilled, cultivated land, gardens, plantations, etc., ; ; ; ; ; ; —Hence,
Trop., ornamented, adorned, polished, elegant, cultivated: milites habebat tam cultos ut argento et auro politis armis ornaret,: adulter,: turba muliebriter culta,: sacerdos veste candidā cultus,: matrona vetitā purpurā culta,: filia cultior,: animi culti,; cf.: tempora et ingenia cultiora,: Tibullus,; cf. carmina,: cultiores doctioresque redire,: sermone cultissimus,.—Adv.: cul-tē, elegantly: dicere, * ; .—Comp.: dicere,; : (sc. veste) progredi, Just. 3, 3, 5: incubare strato lectulo,.—Sup. apparently not in use.

collum, i, n. (ante-class. access. form collus, i, m., Naev., Cato, Lucil., Att., Caecil., Varr. ap. ; ; ; and, acc. to Non. l. l., also :
nec collos mihi Calvus persuaserit,; Front. Ep. ad M.

Meton., of the neck of a flask, bottle, ; ; ; .—Of the poppy, .—Of the middle part of Mount Parnassus, .

cŏlumna, ae, f.
root cel- of excello; v. columen, of which it is orig. a collat. form
.
A projecting object, a column, pillar, post (very freq.), ; ; : columnae et templa et porticus sustinent, tamen habent non plus utilitatis quam dignitatis,; , §§ 133 and 134; : columnae Doricae, Ionicae, Tuscanicae, Corinthiae, Atticae,; sqq.: Rostrata, a column ornamented with beaks of ships, erected in honor of Duellius, the conqueror of the Carthaginians, Spald.; fragments of the inscription on it are yet extant, v. in the Appendix: Maenia, also absol. Columna, a pillory in the Forum Romanum, where thieves, criminal slaves, and debtors were judged and punished, Ascon.—Absol.: ad columnam pervenire. : adhaerescere ad columnam,; cf. Dict. of Antiq. s. v. columna.—Plur.: columnae, as the sign of a bookseller's shop, Orell. ad loc.—From the use of pillars to designate boundaries of countries: Columnae Protei = fines Aegypti,; and: Columnae Herculis, i. e. Calpe et Abyla,; ; , prooem. § 4; .—Prov.: incurrere amentem in columnas,.—*
Trop., a pillar, support; of Augustus, .—
Transf., of objects resembling a pillar; so,
Of the arm (comice): ecce autem aedificat: columnam mento suffigit suo,. —
A water-spout, ; ; .—
Of fire, a meteor, ; cf. of the pillar of cloud and of fire which guided the Exodus,—
Membrum virile, ; ; .—
Narium recta pars eo quod aequaliter sit in longitudine et rotunditate porrecta, columna vocatur, .—*
The top, summit; so only once of the dome of heaven, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 12, 21; cf. columen.

An abode, dwelling in gen. (cf. 1. colo, I. B.), ; and humorously: molarum, for a mill, .—Far more freq.,
(Acc. to colonus, II.) cŏlor (old form cŏlos, like arbos, clamos, honos, etc., ; ; ; , acc. to Prob. II. pp. 1456 and 1467 P.; ; ), ōris, m.
root cal-, to cover; cf.: caligo, occulere, calyx
,
color, hue, tint.
Lit.
In gen.: varii rerum,: nequeunt sine luce Esse,: aureus ignis,: albus,; cf.: color albus praecipue decorus deo est,: purpureus conchyli,: Tyrios mirare,; ; ; cf. ; : colorem accipere,: bibere,: inducere picturae,: color caerulo albidior, viridior et pressior,: amethystinus,: color in pomo est, ubi permaturuit, ater,; : bonus,: melior,: colores, oculos qui pascere possunt,

: rebus nox abstulit atra colorem,: quam cito purpureos deperdit terra colores,: nec varios discet mentiri lana colores,: Iris, Mille trahens varios adverso sole colores,.—Poet.: ducere, of grapes, etc.,to acquire color, become colored,; ; cf. .—

Meton.
Coloring stuff, dyestuff: regionis naturā minii et chrysocollae et aliorum colorum ferax,; —
Flowers of varied colors: aspice quo submittat humus formosa colores,; .—
Specif., the natural color of men, the complexion, tint, hue: qui color, nitor, vestitus,: formae autem dignitas coloris bonitate tuenda est, color exercitationibus corporis,: venusti oculi, color suavis,: verus (opp. to paint), Don.; cf. ; and fucatus,: senex colore mustellino,: niveus,: albus,fair,: egregius,: verecundus,; cf.: vide Num ejus color pudoris signum indicat,: colorem mutare, to change or lose color (on account of any excitement of the passions, from shame, fear, pain, etc.), to blush, etc., ; cf. : color excidit,: perdere,: adeo perturbavit ea vox regem, ut non color, non voltus ei constaret,.—*
Prov.: homo nullius coloris,an unknown man, (like the phrase: albus an ater sit; v. albus).—
Sometimes for beautiful complexion, fine tint, beauty: o formose puer, nimium ne crede colori,: quo fugit Venus, heu, quove color?; .—
Trop.
In gen., color, i.e. external form, state, condition, position, outward show, appearance (predominant in rhet.; v. 2.; elsewh. rare, and mostly poet.): amisimus omnem non modo sucum ac sanguinem, sed etiam colorem et speciem pristinam civitatis,: vitae,; cf.: omnis Aristippum decuit color et status et res, every color became him, i. e. he accommodated himself to every condition, : novimus quosdam, qui multis apud philosophum annis persederint, et ne colorem quidem duxerint, have not acquired even the outward appearance, i.e. have imbibed or learned nothing, ; cf. : omnia eundem ducunt colorem; nec Persis Macedonum mores adumbrare nec Macedonibus Persas imitari indecorum, Vogel ad loc. —
A class, fashion, kind.
In gen. (rare): hos maxime laudat.. egregium hoc quoque, sed secundae sortis ingenium ... hic tertius color est,: tertium illud genus... sed ne hic quidem contemnendus est color tertius,; cf.: in omni vitae colore, prooem. init.—
Esp., of diction, character, fashion, cast, coloring, style: ornatur igitur oratio genere primum et quasi colore quodam et suco suo,; cf. : non unus color prooemii, narrationis, argumentorum, etc.,: qui est, inquit, iste tandem urbanitatis color?: color dicendi maculis conspergitur,; cf.: color totus orationis,: simplicis atque inaffectati gratia,: tragicus,: operum colores,.—
Pregn. (cf. supra, 1. B. 2.), a beautiful, brilliant quality or nature, splendor, lustre, brilliancy (freq. only in rhet. lang.): nullus argento color est avaris Abdito terris,.—
Of diction.
A high, lively coloring, embellishment: intelleges nihil illius (Catonis) lineamentis nisi eorum pigmentorum quae inventa nondum erant, florem et colorem defuisse,; ; (15 a), 2.—
In a bad sense, t. t., an artful concealment of a fault, a pretext, palliation, excuse, Spald.; 6, 5, 5; 10, 1, 116; 11, 1, 81; 12, 1, 33; cf. ; : res illo colore defenditur apud judicem, ut videatur ille non sanae mentis fuisse, etc.,: sub colore adipiscendae possessionis, Cod. Th. 3, 6, 3; .
